Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed consecutive real-world memory-clinic biomarker cohort•September 23, 2026

Real-world amyloid PET yield rises across the clinical continuum

In 194 consecutive memory-clinic patients, amyloid PET positivity rose from 40.9% in subjective cognitive decline to 66.0% in MCI and 91.7% in early Alzheimer disease, while MRI/VSRAD indices added essentially no discrimination beyond clinical diagnosis (cross-validated AUC 0.752 versus 0.751).

Key quantitative results: Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).

Added September 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261490596; PMID:42775784

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The consecutive-clinic design gives useful real-world context for pretest probability and shows that commonly used structural MRI indices did not add amyloid-status discrimination. It supports clinical validity of amyloid PET in the studied setting, not analytical validation or clinical utility: no management-change or outcome endpoint was tested, and positivity in subjective cognitive decline should not be equated with a clinical Alzheimer diagnosis.

Study design

The investigators retrospectively analyzed 194 consecutive patients who underwent florbetapir PET in one memory-clinic setting: 93 with subjective cognitive decline, 47 with MCI and 54 with early Alzheimer disease. Certified visual reads defined positivity; continuous Centiloid and regional SUVR measures quantified burden. MRI/VSRAD indices were available for 153 patients, and models were compared with cross-validated AUC.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).
  • Centiloid values and regional SUVRs increased in parallel across the groups, with the largest regional differences in the temporal cortex and precuneus.
  • Adding MRI/VSRAD indices to the base clinical model did not improve cross-validated discrimination of amyloid positivity: AUC 0.752 with MRI versus 0.751 without it.

What changed

A source-date-new consecutive memory-clinic study now quantifies amyloid PET positivity across subjective cognitive decline, MCI and early Alzheimer disease and directly tests the incremental value of routinely used MRI/VSRAD indices.

Strength of evidence

Moderate real-world clinical-validity evidence from a consecutive cohort with certified reads and cross-validation. The single-center retrospective design, clinically assigned groups, incomplete MRI data and absence of a decision-impact or patient-outcome endpoint limit implementation claims.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The observed gradient can inform pretest-probability discussions, and the near-identical AUCs argue against assuming that VSRAD meaningfully predicts amyloid status beyond clinical classification. PET results still require interpretation in the full clinical context and according to the tracer label.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to amyloid-confirmation pathways, DMT workup discussions and the distinction between structural neurodegeneration markers and amyloid pathology. It also illustrates why a positive scan is not itself a stand-alone clinical diagnosis.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Amyloid status was assigned by certified visual reads and quantified with Centiloids and regional SUVRs. VSRAD MRI indices correlated with amyloid burden but did not improve cross-validated discrimination beyond the clinical group model.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, tracer availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does 40.9% positivity in subjective cognitive decline support screening asymptomatic people?
No. This was a referred memory-clinic cohort, not a population-screening sample, and the study did not test benefits, harms or outcomes from screening.
Did MRI add useful prediction of amyloid positivity?
Not in the cross-validated models: the AUC changed from 0.751 to 0.752 after VSRAD indices were added.
Was clinical utility established?
No. The study measured biomarker prevalence and discrimination; it did not test whether PET-guided decisions changed management or improved outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single-center retrospective cohort with a modest sample
  • Memory-clinic referral population limits generalizability and cannot estimate population screening yield
  • MRI/VSRAD data were available for 153 of 194 participants
  • Clinical categories were not an independent neuropathology reference standard
  • No management-change, decision-impact, cost-effectiveness or patient-outcome endpoint
